title: llm-gemini 0.38
summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.38

Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon. I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse.

Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price, and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires.

The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up:

So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen.

Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st.

I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high.

I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon:

As I've done with several recent models, I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the result.

title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
summary: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
summary: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
summary: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it.
story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. story_key: model:gemini|ver:4|title:introducing gemini 4 neon
content_excerpt: Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . title: claude-code v2.1.328
summary:
What's changed

  • Added auto mode for Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude apps gateway; interactive sessions with no permission mode start in it
  • Added "onFailure": "block" for mcp_tool hooks, as for command and HTTP hooks: a hook whose call fails blocks the action
  • Added a warning when a message from a session that skips permission prompts may be held and dropped by a cloud session
  • Added a notice in /status and claude doctor when an OpenTelemetry exporter has no endpoint and its data would likely be lost
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_DEFERRED_TOOL_RESUME, which lets a host stop claude -p --resume and --continue from running a tool call that a hook deferred
  • Added support for apps that embed Claude Code to switch on the policy plugin's allowManagedModsOnly option; an admin's managed settings still win
  • Added a startup warning to the Claude apps gateway when a policy's maxEffortLevel is not a valid effort level
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --repository-folder to name the folder that sessions use for a repository at --capacity 1, in place of its path under the base folder, which can't be a symbolic link
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a start-up warning when the host's settings.json sets a default permission mode that sessions ignore
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --hook-label to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator, to hand chosen session labels to the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --metadata key=value to claude --environment, to label a session for the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_by_reason_seconds to the orchestrator's /metrics, so a re-opened session's wait can be told from a new one's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added an orchestrator metric, claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_sessions_given_up_total, that counts by cause how often Anthropic gave up starting a runner for a session
  • Fixed Bash commands in zsh stopping with a "not found" error at a word that starts with =, such as echo ==== or [ a == b ]; =cmd no longer expands to a command's path
  • Fixed automatic compaction reusing the session's earlier system prompt instead of rebuilding it the way /compact does
  • Fixed markdown rendering freezing on some very long or malformed input
  • Fixed rare screen freezes
  • Fixed Esc often being lost at a permission prompt or question when you typed straight after it; in terminals that send Alt as Esc and a key, an unused Alt or Option key now declines there
  • Fixed a paste or a terminal's reply being typed into the prompt when a slow connection cut it in two
  • Fixed saving a scheduled task erasing the project's other saved tasks when the scheduled tasks file can't be read, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed a scheduled task with a typo in the project's scheduled tasks file being deleted the next time that file was saved
  • Fixed a case where a resumed cloud session could lose its compaction summary or recent messages when a message was saved late
  • Fixed the token counts on the spinner and for subagents counting a retried reply twice, missing replies that were not streamed, and standing still while Claude thinks
  • Fixed the error shown when usage credits run out mid-response, which named a rate limit
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn outside Claude Desktop with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set behind a gateway rejecting betas, on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry or Claude apps gateway
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS not lengthening the 5-minute connection limit on gateways, custom base URLs and cloud providers
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending for good with "Prompt is too long" after large tool results; the largest are now left out
  • Fixed MCP tools whose input schema starts with anyOf, oneOf or allOf going missing on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed an MCP tool with an invalid input schema failing requests on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off; the tool is now left out and Claude is told why
  • Fixed effort being turned off for a subagent's model for the session if Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Foundry refused its progress summary's effort setting (regression in 2.1.327)
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script when a permission prompt outside auto or bypass mode, a plan approval or a question stayed open for ten minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts in auto and bypass-permissions modes failing to call an MCP server that had connected while the previous script was running
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not running in the background in auto or bypass permissions mode in a session chosen in the claude --resume picker
  • Fixed Code Mode losing a loaded skill, hook context or a note typed with a permission approval when resuming a session in which one reply ran several scripts
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a Code Mode script was cut off when the session was resumed from the picker or in a mode that asks for permission
  • Fixed Code Mode silently using undefined for top-level variables that an earlier failed script never set
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not being told when a failing command's long output was cut
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing valid scripts that start with a { block
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing scripts that use both a top-level await and a top-level return
  • Fixed an @-mentioned small file not being attached in Code Mode after a script had read or written it
  • Fixed Code Mode offering write() and edit() to read-only subagents that can't call them
  • Fixed Claude starting a turn by itself in Code Mode when Esc was followed by a command such as /model
  • Fixed Claude in Code Mode not being told to run workflows only when you ask, or the workflow size you set in /config
  • Fixed Remote Control repeating the same disconnect message, and telling you to retry a session that can't reconnect
  • Fixed a waiting permission prompt being lost, and its answer ignored, when a remote session restarted while the service was slow
  • Fixed cloud sessions resuming a cleared conversation after a rewind followed by /clear
  • Fixed a remote session losing a turn's tool calls and results when its runner or worker was lost after a dropped model stream had been retried
  • Fixed cloud and Remote Control sessions that just started, or have an @ in their title, being unreachable in cross-session messaging from a session with Remote Control on
  • Fixed Claude being told that cloud sessions can never reply; it now learns when a reply can come and how else to get the result
  • Fixed /diff, the Changes pane of Remote Control sessions and the diff beside an edit leaving out committed work after a command moved into another repository
  • Fixed Remote Control not showing a running workflow's agents when a session run by an IDE extension or other SDK app is opened over an hour after the workflow last made progress
  • Remote Control: Fixed an idle Desktop or VS Code session showing as running after Remote Control is turned on
  • Fixed the model saying background agents were still running after an SDK interrupt had stopped them
  • Fixed Send now in the desktop app and SDK hosts telling Claude that a stopped web search found no results
  • Fixed Cmd+letter being typed into the prompt in terminals that report Cmd
  • Fixed Ctrl+click opening a link twice in GNOME Terminal, side mouse buttons acting as clicks, and the first wheel notch in the other direction being ignored after a pause, in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed Shift+Enter in Konsole outside tmux and ssh, and Alt shortcuts on non-Latin keyboard layouts in terminals that speak the kitty keyboard protocol
  • Linux: Fixed pasting in other apps freezing while Claude Code is suspended with Ctrl+Z, when xclip or wl-copy is installed
  • Linux: Fixed Ctrl+V missing the clipboard image, pasting an old one or hanging
  • Fixed text copied in fullscreen mode including the quote bar, losing spaces at line wraps when a drag scrolled upward, or missing words under the "Jump to bottom" pill
  • Fixed an image path pasted into a ! command becoming an attachment
  • Fixed Ctrl+C showing no exit warning while the ? shortcuts list is open
  • Fixed Ctrl+R search in fullscreen mode and the /theme color editor picking the wrong row when keys arrive together, and keys being dropped there and in the search of /config and /plugin
  • Fixed wrong or missing colors inside GNU screen
  • Fixed many background notifications cutting into the top border of open dialogs in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped
  • Fixed Claude calling an artifact private after reading one in a shared folder or publishing to another organization's, and saying only named people can open one when its folder's people can too
  • Fixed a plugin's toast sometimes showing another plugin's text
  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off
  • Fixed agent hooks running past their timeout while compacting after a request was refused as too large
  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number
  • Fixed a crash in secret masking when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the Bash sandbox on Linux renaming .git/HEAD after each command when the branch name is not valid UTF-8
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed all running sessions being stopped when a proxy or web filter answered a poll with HTTP 200 and a body such as {}; the runner now retries such a poll
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed deletion of a kept clone's objects or refs, and of commits that existed only there, after a temporary disk error; that start now fails instead
  • Fixed self-hosted runners stopping when their token ran out on a host whose clock is slow or was set back
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with Anthropic-managed git losing git access to GitHub after a script or hook in the session ran claude again
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with Anthropic-managed git being unable to fetch or push where the machine's git config sets http.proactiveAuth
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner that exited without telling the server when setup failed after it had registered; it now deregisters with a reason, and an on-demand runner reports the failed start
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session not taking effect while it waited for another session to prepare the same repository (--capacity above 1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session with a damaged .claude.json failing every later start under --trust-workspace false; it now starts on defaults, with MCP servers turned off there on again
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start's message losing the words that say what failed when a checkout hook or git printed a lot
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner skipping its post-session hook when a disk stalled for a few seconds; on a dead disk a session's end can take 25 seconds longer by default
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: a session that resumes in a new Claude config directory no longer loses its task list
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a self-hosted session starts without one of its repositories, and why
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --correlation-id of claude --environment not reaching the spawn-runner hook
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner setup wizard's key rotation advice, which now warns that revoking a key stops the sessions running under it
  • Improved claude -p and SDK sessions to fetch managed-settings plugins that have their own git repository, in the background, for a later session
  • Improved how soon managed-settings plugins from a git marketplace load on a fresh machine in claude -p, SDK and Claude Desktop sessions; a short run may exit up to 30 seconds later
  • Improved the time to resume large sessions
  • Improved memory use when resuming a session with many images
  • Improved memory use and response time in long SDK and desktop sessions that run slow commands or tools
  • Improved Code Mode's speed in auto and bypass-permissions modes by removing a 0.75 second pause after most scripts
  • Improved prompt caching for new Code Mode sessions that have MCP servers, and Claude is now told when a server is still connecting and when the list of servers changes
  • Improved Code Mode's token use with shorter tool descriptions
  • Improved Code Mode to show the command a script is running, and its output, while it runs
  • Improved Code Mode edits: an edit that changes nothing no longer stops a script, and Claude is told where a failed edit matches or comes closest
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told which tool calls were still running when a script failed

  • Windows: Improved Code Mode by telling Claude that scripts' shell commands run in Git Bash and that PowerShell aliases run instead of functions with the same name
  • Improved starting several in-process teammates at once: far fewer now fail with "Lock file is already being held"
  • Improved the computer use approval dialog: it now shows each app's level of access and plainer warnings
  • Improved cross-session messaging: Claude now explains that Remote Control is off when a cloud session or another computer is not listed

title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
summary: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
summary: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

title: Why we rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
summary: We reorganized LangSmith around a single agent record. Build, run, improve, and govern every agent from one place, on any framework or runtime.
story_key: story|title:why we rebuilt langsmith around the agent
content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record. When you open an agent record, its traces, evals, Agent Server, and Engine issues are accessible with one click, so you don’t need to navigate multiple surfaces to find them. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows. title: llm 0.37.3
summary:
Release: llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
